arXiv:1412.0132v1 [math.CA] 29 Nov 2014

Total positivity in stable semigroups

Thomas Simon Address: Laboratoire Paul Painlevé, Université Lille 1, Cité Scientifique, F-59655 Villeneuve d’Ascq Cedex. Laboratoire de Physique Théorique et Modèles Statistiques, Université Paris-Sud, F-91405 Orsay. Email: simon@math.univ-lille1.fr
Abstract.

We characterize the total positivity in space-time of strictly stable semigroups on ℝ.{\mathbb{R}}. In the positive case, this solves a problem which had been raised by Karlin. In the drifted Cauchy case, this concludes a study which we had initiated in a previous paper. The case of the isotropic stable semigroup on ℝd{\mathbb{R}}^{d} is also investigated. We apply these results to the bell-shape and monotone likelihood properties of certain stable densities.

Key words and phrases: 
Bell-shape; Cauchy kernel; Fractional integration kernel; Monotone likelihood; Stable density; Stable semigroup; Total positivity; Wronskian.
2010 Mathematics Subject Classification
15B05; 15B48; 26A33; 26A51; 47D07; 60E07

1. Introduction and statement of the results

The strictly stable semigroup on ℝ{\mathbb{R}} is a convolution semigroup whose transition density pα,ρ​(t,x)p_{\alpha,\rho}(t,x) has Fourier transform

(1) ∫ℝpα,ρ​(t,x)​ei​λ​x​𝑑x=e−t​(i​λ)α​e−i​π​α​ρ​sgn​(λ),t>0,λ∈ℝ.\int_{\mathbb{R}}p_{\alpha,\rho}(t,x)e^{{\rm i}\lambda x}\,dx\;=\;e^{-t({\rm i}\lambda)^{\alpha}e^{-{\rm i}\pi\alpha\rho\,{\rm sgn}(\lambda)}},\qquad t>0,\,\lambda\in{\mathbb{R}}.

The convolution property is meant as pα,ρ(t,.)∗pα,ρ(s,.)=pα,ρ(t+s,.)p_{\alpha,\rho}(t,.)\,\ast\,p_{\alpha,\rho}(s,.)\,=\,p_{\alpha,\rho}(t+s,.) for all t,s>0.t,s>0. The parameter α∈(0,2]\alpha\in(0,2] is a self-similarity parameter:

(2) pα,ρ(t,x)=t−1/αpα,ρ(1,xt−1/α),t>0,x∈ℝ.p_{\alpha,\rho}(t,x)\;=\;t^{-1/\alpha}p_{\alpha,\rho}(1,xt^{-1/\alpha}),\qquad t>0,\,x\in{\mathbb{R}}.

Throughout, we will set fα,ρ​(x)=pα,ρ​(1,x).f_{\alpha,\rho}(x)=p_{\alpha,\rho}(1,x). The parameter ρ∈[0,1]\rho\in[0,1] is a positivity parameter:

∫0∞pα,ρ​(t,x)​𝑑x=ρ,t>0.\int_{0}^{\infty}p_{\alpha,\rho}(t,x)\,dx\;=\;\rho,\qquad t>0.

One has the necessary restrictions ρ∈[1−1/α,1/α]\rho\in[1-1/\alpha,1/\alpha] if α>1\alpha>1 and ρ∈(0,1)\rho\in(0,1) if α=1.\alpha=1. If ρ=1/2,\rho=1/2, the right-hand side of (1) reads e−t​|λ|α,e^{-t|\lambda|^{\alpha}}, which is the Fourier transform of the traditional symmetric stable semigroup. If α=2,\alpha=2, then ρ=1/2\rho=1/2 and

(3) p2,1/2​(t,x)=e−x24​t2​π​tp_{2,1/2}(t,x)\;=\;\frac{e^{-\frac{x^{2}}{4t}}}{2\sqrt{\pi t}}

is the standard Gaussian semigroup. It is known that the strictly stable semigroup is up to multiplicative normalization the only convolution semigroup fulfilling a self-similarity property of the type (2). We refer e.g. to [9], Chapter 8 in [1] and Chapter 3 in [10] for more detail on this classical semigroup and the related stable Lévy process.

Of particular interest is the positive stable semi-group pα,1​(t,x)=pα​(t,x),p_{\alpha,1}(t,x)=p_{\alpha}(t,x), which is defined for α∈(0,1),x>0\alpha\in(0,1),x>0 and has a characterization by the Laplace transform:

(4) ∫0∞pα​(t,x)​e−λ​x​𝑑x=e−t​λα,t,λ>0.\int_{0}^{\infty}p_{\alpha}(t,x)e^{-\lambda x}\,dx\;=\;e^{-t\lambda^{\alpha}},\qquad t,\lambda>0.

The importance of the positive stable semigroup stems from its subordination properties. For instance, the transition densities of the semigroup {e−t​(−Δ)α,t>0}\{e^{-t(-\Delta)^{\alpha}},\,t>0\} built on the fractional Laplacian −(−Δ)α-(-\Delta)^{\alpha} on ℝd{\mathbb{R}}^{d} are obtained by the formula

(5) qα,d​(t,z)=∫0∞e−‖z‖24​x​pα​(t,x)​d​x(4​π​x)d/2,t>0,z∈ℝd.q_{\alpha,d}(t,z)\;=\;\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-\frac{||z||^{2}}{4x}}\,p_{\alpha}(t,x)\,\frac{dx}{(4\pi x)^{d/2}},\qquad t>0,\,z\in{\mathbb{R}}^{d}.

A more general result due to Zolotarev shows that every transition density pα,ρ​(t,x)p_{\alpha,\rho}(t,x) on the line can be recovered by a multiplicative convolution of two positive stable densities - see Formula (3.3.16) in [17] which will be recalled in (9) below. Throughout, we will set fα​(x)=pα​(1,x)f_{\alpha}(x)=p_{\alpha}(1,x) and 𝐙α{\bf Z}_{\alpha} for the positive random variable with density fα.f_{\alpha}.

Recall that except for {α=1,ρ∈(0,1)},{α=2,ρ=1/2}\{\alpha=1,\rho\in(0,1)\},\{\alpha=2,\rho=1/2\} and {α=1/2,ρ=1},\{\alpha=1/2,\rho=1\}, the densities pα,ρ​(t,x)p_{\alpha,\rho}(t,x) are not expressed in closed form. Instead, one has convergent series representation given e.g. by (14.30) and (14.31) in [10]. The absence of closed expression makes these densities difficult to study from a classical analytical viewpoint. For instance, it is not even clear from the series representations that the densities are positive.

In this paper, we are interested in the following property extending positivity. Let II be some real interval and KK some real kernel defined on I×II\times I. The kernel KK is called totally positive of order nn (TPn{\rm TP}_{n}) if

(6) det[K⁡(xi,yj)]1≤i,j≤m≥ 0\det\left[K(x_{i},y_{j})\right]_{1\leq i,j\leq m}\;\geq\;0

for every m∈{1,…,n},x1<…<xmm\in\{1,\ldots,n\},\,x_{1}<\ldots<x_{m} and y1<…<ym.y_{1}<\ldots<y_{m}. One says that KK is TP∞{\rm TP}_{\infty} if these inequalities hold for all nn. We refer to [6] for the classic account on this field and its numerous connections with analysis. Let us also mention the recent monograph [8] for a more linear algebraic point of view and updated references. General results on the total positivity in space-time of Markovian kernels are displayed in [6] pp. 43-45. The present paper aims at characterizing this property for the kernels pα,ρ​(t,x)p_{\alpha,\rho}(t,x) with t,x>0.t,x>0. We begin with the positive case.

Theorem 1.

For every n≥2,n\geq 2, one has

pα​(t,x)​is​TPn⇔α∈{1/2,1/3,…,1/n}​or​α<1/n.p_{\alpha}(t,x)\;\,\mbox{{is}}\;\,{\rm TP}_{n}\,\Leftrightarrow\,\alpha\in\{1/2,1/3,\ldots,1/n\}\;\,{\rm or}\;\,\alpha<1/n.

This result solves a problem which has some history. The fact that pα​(t,x)p_{\alpha}(t,x) is TP∞{\rm TP}_{\infty} if and only if α\alpha is the reciprocal of an integer is shown in Paragraph 3.4.(vi) pp.121-122 and 7.12.E p.390 of [6]. In the remaining cases, Karlin asks - see again [6] p.390 - whether pα​(t,x)p_{\alpha}(t,x) is totally positive of some finite order. The fact that pα​(t,x)p_{\alpha}(t,x) is TP2{\rm TP}_{2} if and only if α≤1/2\alpha\leq 1/2 is proved in [12], in connection with the multiplicative strong unimodality of 𝐙α.{\bf Z}_{\alpha}. Finally, the fact that pα​(t,x)∈TPnp_{\alpha}(t,x)\in{\rm TP}_{n} implies α∈{1/2,1/3,…,1/n}\alpha\in\{1/2,1/3,\ldots,1/n\} or α<1/n\alpha<1/n is obtained in the Corollary of [15].

From (2) and Theorem 1.2.1 in [6], the TPn{\rm TP}_{n} character of pα​(t,x)p_{\alpha}(t,x) amounts to that of the convolution kernel fα​(x​y−1).f_{\alpha}(xy^{-1}). As a rule, the TP2{\rm TP}_{2} resp. TP∞{\rm TP}_{\infty} property of a convolution kernel is easier to study, because of its characterization through log-concavity - see Theorem 4.1.8 in [6] - resp. Hadamard factorization - see Theorem 7.3.2 in [6]. On the other hand, there is no such handy criterion for testing TPn{\rm TP}_{n} with n≥3.n\geq 3. Our method relies on an infinite multiplicative factorization of the random variable 𝐙α−α{\bf Z}_{\alpha}^{-\alpha} in terms of renormalized Beta random variables. We prove a local limit theorem, which reduces the problem to the total positivity of the fractional integration kernel

(x−y)+1α−2.(x-y)_{+}^{\frac{1}{\alpha}-2}.

We then apply a result of Karlin on generalized Bessel functions which entails, rather unexpectedly, the right order of total positivity for our kernel pα​(t,x).p_{\alpha}(t,x).

Let us now consider the kernel

Kα​(t,x)=1t2+2​cos⁡(π​α)​t​x+x2=πt​sin⁡(π​α)×p1,α​(t,x)K_{\alpha}(t,x)\;=\;\frac{1}{t^{2}+2\cos(\pi\alpha)tx+x^{2}}\;=\;\frac{\pi}{t\sin(\pi\alpha)}\,\times\,p_{1,\alpha}(t,x)

over (0,+∞)×(0,+∞),(0,+\infty)\times(0,+\infty), with α∈(0,1).\alpha\in(0,1). This can be viewed as a generalization of the classical Cauchy kernel K1/2,K_{1/2}, whose total positivity of infinite order serves as a basic example in [6] p. 149 and is a consequence of Cauchy’s double alternant formula - see also Example 4.3 in [8]. As a consequence of the above result, we prove the following non-trivial characterization.

Corollary 1.

For every n≥2,n\geq 2, one has

Kα​(t,x)​is​TPn⇔α∈{1/2,1/3,…,1/n}​or​α<1/n.K_{\alpha}(t,x)\;\,\mbox{{is}}\;\,{\rm TP}_{n}\,\Leftrightarrow\,\alpha\in\{1/2,1/3,\ldots,1/n\}\;\,{\rm or}\;\,\alpha<1/n.

The characterization of the TP∞{\rm TP}_{\infty} property of KαK_{\alpha} through α∈{1/2,1/3,…,1/n,…}\alpha\in\{1/2,1/3,\ldots,1/n,\ldots\} is obtained in our previous paper [15], thanks to the Hadamard factorization. The fact that Kα​(t,x)∈TPnK_{\alpha}(t,x)\in{\rm TP}_{n} implies α∈{1/2,1/3,…,1/n}\alpha\in\{1/2,1/3,\ldots,1/n\} or α<1/n\alpha<1/n is also proven in [15] with the help of an evaluation of the derivative determinant

det[∂i+j−2Kα​(t,x)∂ti−1​∂xj−1]\det\left[\frac{\partial^{i+j-2}K_{\alpha}(t,x)}{\partial t^{i-1}\partial x^{j-1}}\right]

when t=1t=1 and x→0,x\to 0, by Chebyshev polynomials of the second kind. The reverse inclusion is thoroughly investigated in [15], viewing the derivative determinant as a generating function of alternating sign matrices. In particular, it is shown that the reverse inclusion holds under a plausible hypothesis on this generating function - see Conjecture 4.1 in [15]. However, this hypothesis is difficult to check. It is surprising to the author that the analysis of the non-explicit kernel pα​(t,x)p_{\alpha}(t,x) turns out to be simpler than that of the explicit kernel Kα​(t,x).K_{\alpha}(t,x).

We now state our main result. Introduce the non-negative parameters

γ=1ρ− 1andδ=1ρ​α− 1,\gamma\;=\;\frac{1}{\rho}\,-\,1\qquad\quad\mbox{and}\qquad\quad\delta\;=\;\frac{1}{\rho\alpha}\,-\,1,

and observe that the aforementioned necessary restrictions on (α,ρ)(\alpha,\rho) entail γ≤δ+1.\gamma\leq\delta+1.

Theorem 2.

Assume ρ∈(0,1)\rho\in(0,1) and α<2.\alpha<2. For every n≥2,n\geq 2, one has

pα,ρ​(t,x)​is​TPn⇔(γ,δ)∈ℕ2​or​inf(γ,δ)≥n−1.p_{\alpha,\rho}(t,x)\;\,\mbox{{is}}\;\,{\rm TP}_{n}\,\Leftrightarrow\,(\gamma,\delta)\in{\mathbb{N}}^{2}\;\;{\rm or}\;\;\inf(\gamma,\delta)\geq n-1.

Notice that the assumption made on (α,ρ)(\alpha,\rho) is no restriction. Indeed, when ρ=0\rho=0 the kernel is zero, whereas the case ρ=1\rho=1 is the matter of Theorem 1 and the case α=2\alpha=2 yields the Gaussian kernel (3) which is known to be TP∞{\rm TP}_{\infty} by Formula 3 (1.5) p.100 in [6]. Observe finally that for α=1\alpha=1 the result is already contained in Corollary 1, since γ=δ.\gamma=\delta. The following figure illustrates our results, the bold points meaning TP∞.{\rm TP}_{\infty}.

We finally turn our attention to the kernel

ρα,d​(t,r)=∫0∞e−r24​x​pα​(t,x)​d​x(4​π​x)d/2,t,r>0,\rho_{\alpha,d}(t,r)\;=\;\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-\frac{r^{2}}{4x}}\,p_{\alpha}(t,x)\,\frac{dx}{(4\pi x)^{d/2}},\qquad t,r>0,

which is the radial part of the transition density qα,d​(t,z)q_{\alpha,d}(t,z) on ℝd.{\mathbb{R}}^{d}. The following can be viewed as a multidimensional generalization of Theorem 2, in the case ρ=1/2.\rho=1/2.

Corollary 2.

For every n≥2,n\geq 2, one has

ρα,d​(t,r)​is​TPn⇔α∈{1/2,1/3,…,1/n}​or​α<1/n.\rho_{\alpha,d}(t,r)\;\,\mbox{{is}}\;\,{\rm TP}_{n}\,\Leftrightarrow\,\alpha\in\{1/2,1/3,\ldots,1/n\}\;\,{\rm or}\;\,\alpha<1/n.

The if part of the proof of Theorem 2 resp. Corollary 2 is a rather straightforward consequence of Theorem 1 and Zolotarev’s aforementioned factorization resp. the chi-square factorization which is obtained from (5). The only if part is more delicate and relies on an asymptotic analysis of the derivative determinant, in the same spirit as our previous papers [14, 15]. These proofs are given in the next section after the proofs of Theorem 1 and Corollary 1. In the third section, we apply some of these results to two visual features of real stable densities: the bell-shape and the monotone likelihood property.

2. Proofs

2.1. Proof of Theorem 1

𝐗α,n=eγ⁡(α−1)×∏k=0neψ⁡(1+kα)−ψ⁡(1+kα)​𝐁1+kα,1α−1{\bf X}_{\alpha,n}\;=\;e^{\gamma(\alpha-1)}\,\times\,\prod_{k=0}^{n}e^{\psi(1+\frac{k}{\alpha})-\psi(\frac{1+k}{\alpha})}\,{\bf B}_{1+\frac{k}{\alpha},\frac{1}{\alpha}-1}

supx>0|gα​(x)−gα,n​(x)|→ 0as n→+∞.\sup_{x>0}|g_{\alpha}(x)-g_{\alpha,n}(x)|\;\to\;0\qquad\mbox{{as} $n\to+\infty.$}

We can now finish the proof of Theorem 1. Again by Theorem 1.2.1 in [6], we must show that the kernel

gα(xy−1)=y1+1/αα​x1+1/αfα(y1/αx−1/α)g_{\alpha}(xy^{-1})\;=\;\frac{y^{1+1/\alpha}}{\alpha x^{1+1/\alpha}}\,f_{\alpha}(y^{1/\alpha}x^{-1/\alpha})

This kernel is of the multiplicative convolution type and applying repeatedly Lemma 3.1.1 in [6], we see that it is sufficient to prove that

Remark 1.

3. Applications to stable densities

In this section, we investigate further analytical properties of the real stable densities

fα,ρ​(x)=pα,ρ​(1,x).f_{\alpha,\rho}(x)\;=\;p_{\alpha,\rho}(1,x).

Let us again refer to [17] for a thorough presentation of these densities, which are of constant use in probability and statistics. In Zolotarev’s opinion, stable densities should also be accorded civil rights in the theory of special functions - see Section 2.10 in [17]. However, in the absence of closed formulæ, some of their basic properties are still unknown, or at least unproven.

3.1. Bell-shape

A smooth density function on a real interval whose derivatives vanish at both ends of the interval is said to be bell-shaped if its nn-th derivative vanishes exactly nn times inside the interval, for every n≥0.n\geq 0. In the following, we will use the notation BSn{\rm BS}_{n} if the property holds for every kk-th derivative with k≤n.k\leq n. For example, a BS2{\rm BS}_{2} density is strictly positive, strictly unimodal and successively convex, concave and convex like the familiar bell curve. There is a tight connection between bell-shape and total positivity which is exemplified by the notion of ETP kernel - see Paragraph 6.11.C in [6]. In a previous paper [16], to which we refer for more details, references and open questions around the bell-shape, we have shown that all densities fαf_{\alpha} are in BS∞.{\rm BS}_{\infty}.

In this paragraph, we apply our previous results to the BSn{\rm BS}_{n} property of the symmetric density qα​(x)=qα,1​(x)=fα,1/2​(x).q_{\alpha}(x)=q_{\alpha,1}(x)=f_{\alpha,1/2}(x). It is easily seen by Fourier inversion that

qα​(x)=1π​∫0∞cos⁡(t​x)​e−t2​α​𝑑tq_{\alpha}(x)\;=\;\frac{1}{\pi}\int_{0}^{\infty}\cos(tx)\,e^{-t^{2\alpha}}\,dt

is real analytic with all derivatives vanishing at infinity. Moreover it is strictly positive on ℝ{\mathbb{R}} and strictly unimodal by Yamazato’s theorem - see Theorem 53.1 in [10] and also [13] for a short proof, hence it is BS1.{\rm BS}_{1}. Let us prove the following reinforcement.

Proposition 1.

For every n≥2,n\geq 2, the function qαq_{\alpha} is BSn{\rm BS}_{n} if α∈{1/2,1/3,…,1/n}\alpha\in\{1/2,1/3,\ldots,1/n\} or α<1/n.\alpha<1/n.

Proof.

By an induction and a successive application of Rolle’s theorem, it is clear that qα(n)q_{\alpha}^{(n)} vanishes and changes its sign at least nn times on ℝ,{\mathbb{R}}, since qα(n−1)q_{\alpha}^{(n-1)} vanishes at infinity. On the other hand, differentiating (5) shows after a change of variable that

qα(n)​(x)=(−1)n2​π​∫0∞e−x2​z−2​Hn​(x​z−1)​pα​(z2/4)​z−n​𝑑zq_{\alpha}^{(n)}(x)\;=\;\frac{(-1)^{n}}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-x^{2}z^{-2}}H_{n}(xz^{-1})\,p_{\alpha}(z^{2}/4)\,z^{-n}dz

for all x∈ℝ,n≥0,x\in{\mathbb{R}},n\geq 0, where HnH_{n} is the n−n-th Hermite polynomial. In particular, for every p≥0p\geq 0 one has qα(2​p+1)​(0)=0.q_{\alpha}^{(2p+1)}(0)=0. Recalling that qαq_{\alpha} is even and putting everything together, we are hence reduced to show that for every n≥2n\geq 2, the function qα(n)q_{\alpha}^{(n)} vanishes at most [n+12][\frac{n+1}{2}] times on (0,+∞)(0,+\infty) as soon as α∈{1/2,1/3,…,1/n}\alpha\in\{1/2,1/3,\ldots,1/n\} or α<1/n.\alpha<1/n.

Fix n≥2n\geq 2 and assume α∈{1/2,1/3,…,1/n}\alpha\in\{1/2,1/3,\ldots,1/n\} or α<1/n.\alpha<1/n. A further change of variable implies

(11) qα(k)​(x)=(−1)n2​π​∫0∞e−z2​zk−2​Hk​(z)​pα​(x2/4​z2)​𝑑zq_{\alpha}^{(k)}(x)\;=\;\frac{(-1)^{n}}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-z^{2}}z^{k-2}H_{k}(z)\,p_{\alpha}(x^{2}/4z^{2})\,dz

for all x,k>0.x,k>0. It is known that the function e−z2​zn−2​Hn​(z)e^{-z^{2}}z^{n-2}H_{n}(z) vanishes exactly [n+12][\frac{n+1}{2}] times on (0,+∞).(0,+\infty). Since [n+12]≤n−1,[\frac{n+1}{2}]\leq n-1, we can deduce from (11), Theorem 1 and Schoenberg’s variation-diminishing property - see Theorem 1.3.1(a) in [6] - that qα(n)q_{\alpha}^{(n)} changes its sign at most [n+12][\frac{n+1}{2}] times inside (0,+∞),(0,+\infty), the zero terms being discarded. Suppose now that qα(n)q_{\alpha}^{(n)} would vanish on (0,+∞)(0,+\infty) without changing its sign. By analyticity, this zero would be isolated and we can again apply Rolle’s theorem to deduce that qα(n+1)q_{\alpha}^{(n+1)} would change its sign at least 1+[n+22]1+[\frac{n+2}{2}] times. However, since [n+22]≤n−1,[\frac{n+2}{2}]\leq n-1, this is a contradiction because the same argument as above shows that qα(n+1)q_{\alpha}^{(n+1)} changes its sign at most [n+22][\frac{n+2}{2}] times. This completes the proof.

Remark 4.

A direct analysis shows that the Cauchy density

q1/2,1​(x)=f1,1/2​(x)=1π⁡(1+x2)q_{1/2,1}(x)\;=\;f_{1,1/2}(x)\;=\;\frac{1}{\pi(1+x^{2})}

is BS∞,{\rm BS}_{\infty}, and by translation the same property holds for all densities p1,ρ.p_{1,\rho}. It is very natural to conjecture that all densities fα,ρf_{\alpha,\rho} are BS∞.{\rm BS}_{\infty}. This is claimed in [4], with unfortunately a serious mistake in the proof - see Section 3.3 in [16] for details. The above proposition is based on the subordination method and can be extended to some densities fα,ρf_{\alpha,\rho} with α<1,\alpha<1, but Theorem 1 clearly shows the limits of this method. To prove the conjecture, an additive factorization like the one used in [16] could be the right approach, eventhough the situation is more complicated on the line than on the half-line.

3.2. Monotone likelihood property

An absolutely continuous positive random variable XX is said to have the single intersection property if the density functions of XX and c​XcX meet exactly once for every c∈(0,1)∪(1,∞).c\in(0,1)\cup(1,\infty). This can be viewed as a refinement as the usual stochastic ordering between XX and c​X.cX. An absolutely continuous real random variable YY is said to have the double intersection property if the density functions of YY and c​YcY meet exactly twice for every c∈(0,1)∪(1,∞).c\in(0,1)\cup(1,\infty). In the symmetric integrable case, this implies a convex ordering between YY and c​Y.cY. In the following, we will use the same intersection terminology for a given density as for a random variable. We refer to [11] for more information on intersection properties for densities and stochastic orderings between random variables.

It was shown in [6] that fαf_{\alpha} has the single intersection property and that qαq_{\alpha} has the double intersection property - see Theorems 4.1 and 4.2 therein. The following proposition, whose proof is independent of the previous results, completes the picture.

Proposition 2.

The density fα,ρf_{\alpha,\rho} has the double intersection property as soon as ρ∈(0,1).\rho\in(0,1).

Proof.

With our above notation, it is enough to show that both positive random variables 𝐗α,ρ+{\bf X}^{+}_{\alpha,\rho} and 𝐗α,1−ρ+{\bf X}^{+}_{\alpha,1-\rho} have the single intersection property. Indeed, the first one is distributed according as the positive branch of fα,ρf_{\alpha,\rho}, whereas the second one is distributed according as the negative branch of fα,ρ.f_{\alpha,\rho}. Since both branches are analytic on (0,+∞),(0,+\infty), the principle of isolated zeroes and a perusal of the proofs of Lemma 3.1 and Theorem 3.1 imply that we are reduced to prove the unimodality of the random variables log⁡𝐗α,ρ+\log{\bf X}^{+}_{\alpha,\rho} and log⁡𝐗α,1−ρ+.\log{\bf X}^{+}_{\alpha,1-\rho}. By (9) and the aforementioned Yamazato theorem, it is enough to show that log⁡𝐙β\log{\bf Z}_{\beta} is self-decomposable for every β∈(0,1).\beta\in(0,1). This well-known fact is a consequence of the Fourier transform

𝔼⁡[ei​s​log⁡𝐙β]=exp⁡[i​γ​(1−1/β)​s+∫−∞0(ei​s​x−1−i​s​x)​e−β​|x|​(1−e−(1−β)​|x|)|x|​(1−e−|x|)​(1−e−β​|x|)​𝑑x]{\mathbb{E}}[e^{{\rm i}s\log{\bf Z}_{\beta}}]\;=\;\exp\left[{\rm i}\gamma(1-1/\beta)s\;+\;\int_{-\infty}^{0}(e^{{\rm i}sx}-1-{\rm i}sx)\,\frac{e^{-\beta|x|}(1-e^{-(1-\beta)|x|})}{|x|(1-e^{-|x|})(1-e^{-\beta|x|})}\,dx\right]

which was used in the proof of Theorem 1, the easily established increasing character of

x↦e−β​|x|​(1−e−(1−β)​|x|)(1−e−|x|)​(1−e−β​|x|)x\;\mapsto\;\frac{e^{-\beta|x|}(1-e^{-(1-\beta)|x|})}{(1-e^{-|x|})(1-e^{-\beta|x|})}

on (−∞,0),(-\infty,0), and Corollary 15.11 in [10].

∎

Following Section 5 in [6], a real density function ff is said to have the monotone likelihood ratio (MLR) property in (0,+∞)(0,+\infty) if the function x↦f⁡(x)/f⁡(c​x)x\mapsto f(x)/f(cx) is monotone on (0,+∞)(0,+\infty) for every c∈(0,1)∪(1,∞).c\in(0,1)\cup(1,\infty). In the case of strict monotonicity, this property is clearly a reinforcement of the single intersection property. The Karlin-Rubin theorem - see e.g. Theorem 8.4.1 in [7] - establishes a well-known connection between the MLR property and the construction of certain UMP tests. It is observed in Section 5 [6] that none of the functions fαf_{\alpha} and qαq_{\alpha} has the MLR property in general. We can show the following characterization, which somehow contradicts the introduction in [6].

Proposition 3.

The density fα,ρf_{\alpha,\rho} has the MLR property in (0,+∞)(0,+\infty) if and only if one of the three following disjoint conditions is fulfilled: {inf(γ,δ)≥1},{γ=0,δ≥1},{γ=1,δ=0}.\{\inf(\gamma,\delta)\geq 1\},\,\{\gamma=0,\;\delta\geq 1\},\,\{\gamma=1,\;\delta=0\}.

Proof.

As observed in the beginning of Section 5 in [6], the MLR property of a density ff on (0,+∞)(0,+\infty) is equivalent to the TP2{\rm TP}_{2} character of the kernel f⁡(x​y−1)f(xy^{-1}) on (0,+∞)×(0,+∞).(0,+\infty)\times(0,+\infty). The result is hence a direct consequence of Theorems 1 and 2.

∎

In the positive case ρ=1,\rho=1, the MLR property of fαf_{\alpha} is hence characterized by α≤1/2,\alpha\leq 1/2, which is the main result of [12]. Since fαf_{\alpha} is smooth, it is easily proved - see again [12] - that the MLR property of fαf_{\alpha} amounts to the non-increasing character of

(12) x↦x​fα′​(x)fα​(x)x\;\mapsto\;\frac{xf_{\alpha}^{\prime}(x)}{f_{\alpha}(x)}

on (0,+∞).(0,+\infty). It is interesting to ask how this function varies when α>1/2,\alpha>1/2, and we believe that it decreases and then increases. The following last proposition provides a partial answer.

Proposition 4.

When α>1/2,\alpha>1/2, the function in (12) decreases on (0,mα],(0,m_{\alpha}], where mαm_{\alpha} is the unique positive mode of fα.f_{\alpha}.

Proof.

We only sketch the proof, which depends on some of the material displayed in Chapter 10 of [10]. Differentiating three times Steutel’s integro-differential equation, we have

(x​fα′′​(x)+fα′​(x))​fα​(x)−x​(fα′​(x))2=α​fα​(x)Γ⁡(1−α)​∫0∞fα​(x−y)​(fα′​(x)fα​(x)−fα′​(x−y)fα​(x−y))​y−α​𝑑y(xf_{\alpha}^{\prime\prime}(x)+f_{\alpha}^{\prime}(x))f_{\alpha}(x)\,-\,x(f_{\alpha}^{\prime}(x))^{2}\;=\;\frac{\alpha f_{\alpha}(x)}{\Gamma(1-\alpha)}\int_{0}^{\infty}f_{\alpha}(x-y)\left(\frac{f_{\alpha}^{\prime}(x)}{f_{\alpha}(x)}-\frac{f_{\alpha}^{\prime}(x-y)}{f_{\alpha}(x-y)}\right)\,y^{-\alpha}\,dy

for every x>0x>0. See Formula (53.13) in [10], which is proved there only for a certain class of self-decomposable densities, but it is easily extended to fαf_{\alpha} by approximation. On the other hand, we know that fαf_{\alpha} is log-concave on (0,mα](0,m_{\alpha}] by the Yamazato property - see Lemma 53.2 (iii) in [10] and observe that this is again easily extended to fα.f_{\alpha}. This implies that the right-hand side in the above equation is negative for every x∈(0,mα].x\in(0,m_{\alpha}]. Hence, the function in (12) decreases on (0,mα].(0,m_{\alpha}].

∎

Remark 5.

This proposition implies that the function fα​(x)/fα​(c​x)f_{\alpha}(x)/f_{\alpha}(cx) increases on (0,mα/c](0,m_{\alpha}/c] for any c>1c>1 and decreases on (0,mα](0,m_{\alpha}] for any c<1.c<1. This can be viewed as partial MLR property when α>1/2.\alpha>1/2.
